summary: This standards-track RFC defines NAT traversal for datagram media streams that are set up and controlled with RTSP 2.0. It adapts Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) to use RTSP as its signaling channel, defining the needed RTSP extensions and procedures.

eli5.summary: Streaming from behind a home router is like delivering to an apartment with no door number. This teaches a streaming system how to find a way in.

questions: how does ice work with rtsp
how does rtsp work behind a nat
what does rtsp 480 ice connectivity check failure mean
subtitle: How a streaming server and a client behind a NAT use ICE, carried over RTSP, to find a media path that works.

tldr.problem: RTSP sets up media streams that the server sends to the client, and NATs make it hard for those datagrams to reach the right host. Sending media to whatever address a request names also lets attackers aim a server at a victim.
tldr.mechanism: The client and server swap ICE candidates, usernames and passwords inside RTSP SETUP messages, then run STUN connectivity checks. The server only plays media after the checks succeed.
tldr.outcome: Media can traverse NATs, and the checks confirm the client really wants the stream. The scope is datagram media only; NAT problems for the RTSP signaling itself are left for future study.

today: RFC 7825 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2016, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RTSP 2.0 in RFC 7826.

sections.title: Why RTSP Media Needs NAT Traversal
sections.content:
The Real-Time Streaming Protocol (RTSP) sets up and controls media streams that are delivered to receivers. That stream setup is what causes trouble with Network Address Translators (NATs) unless the protocol adds extra provisions. RFC 7826 defines RTSP 2.0, and this document builds on it because RTSP 2.0 has a well-defined extension mechanism. RTSP 1.0 did not, so a backwards-compatible extension was not possible there.

After an evaluation of candidate solutions in RFC 7604, the authors chose a mechanism based on Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE, RFC 5245). The RFC gives two reasons: it supports RTSP servers behind NATs, and it mitigates the risk of RTSP servers being used as Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attack tools.

The scope is limited. The design is optimized for media delivery from server to client, and the NAT problem for RTSP signaling traffic is left for future study. The ICE usage here is called ICE-RTSP. It is slightly simpler than full ICE for SIP/SDP, and it is not ICE-Lite.
sections.eli5: Streaming from a server to a home behind a router is like sending a parcel to a flat with no door number. This RFC teaches the two sides to find the right door before the parcel is sent.

sections.title: How the Exchange Works
sections.content:
The server should advertise ICE support with a new SDP attribute, a=rtsp-ice-d-m, and with a new feature tag, setup.ice-d-m. The client then gathers candidate addresses for each media stream and runs a STUN server on each local candidate's transport address.

In its SETUP request the client offers a transport specification with the new D-ICE lower layer and a candidates parameter. The server gathers its own candidates and answers with 200 OK, selecting the ICE transport and listing its candidates. The server starts connectivity checks, the client starts its own, and when a client check reaches the server it triggers a check back from the server.

When the client has finished its checks and nominated candidates, it can send PLAY. The server checks that its own connectivity checks concluded successfully and only then plays the stream. Afterwards, the client keeps using STUN as a keep-alive for the used candidate pairs so the NAT bindings stay current. Servers behind NATs also send keep-alives when they are not sending media.
sections.eli5: Both sides swap lists of possible addresses, then send little test messages to each address. Only when a test message gets through does the show begin.

sections.title: The RTSP Extensions
sections.content:
The D-ICE lower layer is for datagram transport that can be told apart from STUN messages. UDP candidates MUST be supported, and TCP candidates (RFC 6544) are OPTIONAL. Four combinations are defined: RTP/AVP/D-ICE, RTP/AVPF/D-ICE, RTP/SAVP/D-ICE and RTP/SAVPF/D-ICE. A D-ICE transport specification MUST include unicast, MUST include candidates, MUST NOT include dest_addr, and SHALL include ICE-Password and ICE-ufrag.

Each candidates entry carries a foundation, a component ID, a transport, a priority, an address, a port and a candidate type (host, srflx, prflx or relay), plus related address and port for non-host candidates. For RTP, component 1 is RTP and component 2 is RTCP, unless RTP and RTCP are multiplexed.

The username fragment and password are chosen randomly at the start of a session. The ICE-ufrag MUST have at least 24 bits of randomness and the ICE-Password at least 128 bits, which means at least 4 and 22 characters, and values may be up to 256 characters.

Two new RTSP status codes are defined: 150 (server still working on ICE connectivity checks) and 480 (ICE connectivity check failure). A new PLAY_NOTIFY reason, ice-restart, is also defined.
sections.eli5: The RFC adds a few new labels to RTSP messages: a list of addresses, a secret word and password for the test messages, and two new status messages that say 'still checking' or 'checking failed'.

sections.title: Checks, Nomination and Restarts
sections.content:
A server that is publicly reachable MAY use a high-reachability configuration. It offers one candidate per address family, media stream and component, and may hold back its own checks until a client check triggers one. It must still send binding requests, because it has to verify that the client is present and wants the media. This removes the threat that a SETUP request triggers a large number of STUN checks toward arbitrary addresses. Full ICE-Lite is not allowed: the ICE-Lite attribute SHALL NOT be used with RTSP, because Lite does not make the server send a check.

The client is the controlling party. It SHOULD use aggressive nomination during the initial SETUP, since media only starts after PLAY. If the server cannot conclude its checks when PLAY arrives, it replies 150, first within 200 milliseconds and then every 3 seconds, until it can give a final answer. A failure gets 480. A 480 in reply to SETUP means no candidate pair could be built. The server MUST NOT free its candidates after a 480 to PLAY.

A new SETUP with a new username fragment and password restarts ICE, and the server SHALL accept such a SETUP in the PLAY state. If the session is already playing, the checks SHALL use regular nomination and media continues on the old pair until the new pair is nominated. If the server's address changes, for example through load balancing or a failure, it SHALL send PLAY_NOTIFY with ice-restart, and the client then gathers new candidates and sends SETUP for each media stream.
sections.eli5: If the server is still testing, it keeps saying 'one moment' every few seconds. If the test fails, it says so. If the server has to move house in the middle of the show, it tells the client, and they redo the tests.

sections.title: Proxies, Multiplexing and Fallback
sections.content:
A media-handling proxy splits the media path in two, and the NAT traversal runs on each leg. Such proxies are RECOMMENDED to support this specification. A signaling-only proxy must forward SETUP requests with the D-ICE transport and related parameters unchanged. A proxy that supports ICE SHALL list setup.ice-d-m in the Proxy-Supported header. A media-handling proxy without ICE support is assumed to drop the D-ICE transport and fall back to a lower-priority one, so clients SHOULD list the D-ICE transport first and RECOMMENDED fallbacks after it. Using the feature tag in Proxy-Require is NOT RECOMMENDED, because the result varies by proxy type.

Clients and servers that support D-ICE with RTP SHALL also implement RTP and RTCP multiplexing (RFC 5761). This needs only one component per media stream, which removes at least one STUN check per stream and halves the number of STUN instances and their state.

When the server is not ICE capable, a client may use part of ICE for fallback. For that case the RFC advises a relay-based address as the default fallback, or a STUN-derived server-reflexive address if no relay is available, and warns that the reflexive approach is brittle.
sections.eli5: Some helpers in the middle of the route may not know the new trick. The client therefore lists a plain method as a backup, and the two ends pack their two kinds of messages through one door to save work.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The main threat is a flood of media sent to a victim. An attacker could craft RTSP SETUP requests naming a victim's address, and many hosts behind NATs or firewalls do not answer unsolicited packets with an ICMP port unreachable error. ICE protects against this: the connectivity check gives the server confirmation that the client wants the media. Simply requiring that SDP addresses match the signaling address would not protect other hosts behind the same NAT, would prevent separating an RTSP controller from a playout device, and would force proxies to relay media.

RTSP signaling SHOULD be protected with TLS to prevent eavesdropping and modification. The STUN amplification attack from RFC 5245 needs consideration; servers using the high-reachability option mitigate it well, since they only send checks toward an address and port from which they received a check.

The RFC also notes that NAT translation logs help analysts but can be large and privacy invasive, so procedures for log flushing and privacy protection SHALL be in place.
sections.eli5: Without the tests, a bad person could trick the server into blasting video at someone who never asked for it. The tests make sure the receiver says 'yes, I want this' first.

messages.label: SETUP with D-ICE and candidates
messages.note: Includes ICE-ufrag, ICE-Password and the client's candidates.

messages.label: 200 OK with candidates
messages.note: Selects the D-ICE transport and lists the server's candidates.

messages.label: STUN connectivity checks
messages.note: A high-reachability server may wait for a triggered check.

messages.label: STUN connectivity checks
messages.note: Client checks trigger checks from the server.

messages.label: PLAY
messages.note: Sent once the client's checks have concluded.

messages.label: 150 or 480 or 200 OK
messages.note: 150 while checks run, 480 on failure, 200 OK when media starts.

items.label: Server still working on ICE connectivity checks
items.desc: Used with PLAY; sent within 200 ms, then every 3 seconds.

items.label: ICE Connectivity check failure
items.desc: Used with PLAY and SETUP when checks fail or no candidate pair exists.

items.label: PLAY_NOTIFY Notify-Reason
items.desc: Tells the client an ICE restart is needed.

items.label: Feature tag
items.desc: Signals support for all mandatory functions of this specification.

items.label: SDP attribute
items.desc: Session-level attribute that advertises server ICE support.
